issues.legal_issue: A separate suit cannot be used to set aside a consent decree on the ground that the compromise was unlawful, including because consent was allegedly obtained by fraud or misrepresentation.
material_facts: The suit sought to declare a compromise decree invalid, sham, collusive, and unenforceable.
The plaintiffs alleged that they signed the compromise after being told it would merely protect family property from bank claims and would not affect their rights.
The allegations therefore challenged the compromise as voidable for want of free consent.
The challenge was brought in a separate suit rather than before the court that recorded the compromise.
issues.conclusion: The separate suit was barred. A party seeking to challenge the lawfulness of a compromise must raise the issue before the court that recorded it.
issues.legal_principle: Order XXIII Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure, including its proviso and Explanation, requires the court recording a compromise to decide a dispute about its lawfulness; an agreement void or voidable under the Indian Contract Act, 1872 is not lawful for this purpose. Sections 10, 14 and 19 of the Contract Act address valid agreements, free consent and voidability. Order XXIII Rule 3A bars a separate suit to set aside a decree on the ground that its compromise was unlawful. Banwari Lal v. Chando Devi, Pushpa Devi Bhagat v. Rajinder Singh, R. Rajanna v. S.R. Venkataswamy, and Triloki Nath Singh v. Anirudh Singh establish that the challenge must be made to the court that recorded the compromise.

rule.if: separate_suit_challenging_consent_decree and challenge_claims_compromise_was_unlawful and (challenge_alleges_fraud_or_misrepresentation or challenge_alleges_other_invalid_consent)

predicates.separate_suit_challenging_consent_decree: A party to a consent decree brought a separate suit seeking to set it aside.
predicates.challenge_claims_compromise_was_unlawful: The separate suit alleged that the compromise underlying the decree was unlawful.
predicates.challenge_alleges_fraud_or_misrepresenta: The party alleged that fraud or misrepresentation caused them to agree to the compromise.
predicates.challenge_alleges_other_invalid_consent: The party alleged another defect that made consent to the compromise invalid.

issues.definition: When a party separately sues to set aside a consent decree for an alleged defect in the compromise, the separate suit is barred if the challenge alleges fraud, misrepresentation, or another basis for treating the compromise as unlawful.

issues.legal_issue: A claim for partition may proceed as to property omitted from an earlier compromise decree, and branches of a family are entitled to equal shares where the evidence establishes that the family remained joint when the property was acquired for their benefit.
material_facts: A registered partition had earlier divided property among three family branches.
After that partition, the branches continued to live together, acquired property jointly, and carried on family businesses together.
A family member later asserted that a further division of the branches’ properties had been agreed, but the asserted agreement was not produced or proved.
The disputed residential property was not included in the earlier partition suit or compromise decree.

The property was acquired in one member’s name, but the purchase money came from a company whose shareholders and directors included members of all three branches; the purchaser did not show that the amount was repaid.
The court found that the family remained joint when the property was acquired and that the property was acquired for the benefit of all three branches.
issues.conclusion: The earlier compromise decree did not bar a partition claim concerning the omitted property. Each of the three branches was entitled to an equal share, and a preliminary partition decree was directed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Hindu law, a divided family may reunite, but reunion requires an intention to reunite in estate and interest and must be strictly proved; that intention may be inferred from conduct of an unequivocal character. Mere joint residence or trading alone is insufficient. Bhagwan Dayal v. Reoti Devi, relying on Palani Ammal v. Muthuvenkatacharla Moniagar, states that the burden of proving reunion is heavy and that the conduct must necessarily imply an agreement to reunite. Mukku Venkataramayya v. Mukku Tatayya and Anil Kumar Mitra v. Ganendra Nath Mitra also address proof of reunion through conduct. A property omitted from the earlier decree is not barred from a partition claim merely because that decree cannot be challenged in a separate suit.

rule.if: partition_claim_for_property and property_omitted_from_prior_compromise_decree and prior_formal_partition and post_partition_joint_family_conduct and later_division_asserted_by_family_member and purchase_funded_by_company_owned_across_branches

predicates.partition_claim_for_property: A party brought a proceeding seeking partition of a property.
predicates.property_omitted_from_prior_compromise_d: The property claimed for partition was not included in the earlier compromise decree.
predicates.prior_formal_partition: The family members had previously recorded a formal division of property.
predicates.post_partition_joint_family_conduct: After the formal division, family members continued to live together, acquire property together, or conduct family businesses together.
predicates.later_division_asserted_by_family_member: A family member asserted that a further division of the family properties had been agreed.
predicates.purchase_funded_by_company_owned_across_: The property was acquired in one member’s name using funds from a company in which members of the family branches held interests.

issues.definition: If a partition claim concerns property omitted from an earlier compromise decree and the evidence shows continued joint-family conduct after a prior division, a later asserted division, and acquisition funding from a company owned across the branches, the branches are entitled to equal shares.
